title: Where are you going?
goal: Tell walking apart from riding, ask for directions in the street, and use *do*, *na* and *w* for destinations.
bekal: asking for and understanding simple directions
naming a destination with the right preposition

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jak dojść do dworca?
dialogs.intro: A sidewalk in the city center. Budi stops a passerby, holding a phone with a dead battery.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.text: Idzie pan prosto, a potem w lewo przy kościele.
lines.id: Go straight ahead, then turn left at the church.
lines.literal: walks sir straight, and then to left by church.

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.text: Jakieś dziesięć minut pieszo. Albo jedzie pan tramwajem numer cztery.
lines.id: About ten minutes on foot. Or take tram number four.
lines.literal: about ten minutes on-foot. or rides sir by-tram number four.

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.id: Around the corner, on the right.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Czy ten tramwaj jedzie też na lotnisko?
lines.id: Does that tram go to the airport too?
lines.literal: whether this tram rides also to airport?

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.text: Nie, na lotnisko jedzie pociąg z dworca głównego.
lines.id: No, a train goes to the airport from the main station.
lines.literal: no, to airport rides train from station main.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How much is a train ticket?

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.text: Nie wiem dokładnie. Chyba siedemnaście złotych.
lines.id: I'm not exactly sure. Seventeen złoty, I think.
lines.literal: not I-know exactly. probably seventeen złoty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you so much for your help!

lines.speaker: Przechodzień:
lines.text: Nie ma za co. Miłego dnia!
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a nice day!
lines.literal: not is for what. nice day!

notes: **Iść or jechać?** Polish has no single word for "go". *Iść* is for going **on foot**, *jechać* for going **by vehicle** — bus, car, train, bike. Using the wrong one won't stop people understanding you, but it sounds foreign straight away.

**Idzie pan prosto** — note the form *idzie* (the "he" form), not *idziesz*. With *pan* and *pani* you always use the third person, a rule you met in unit 1. It's also a gentle way to give directions: literally "the gentleman walks straight", not an order.

**Do dworca, na lotnisko, w lewo.** Three prepositions for three kinds of destination. Rough pattern: *do* for buildings and towns (*do sklepu*, *do Krakowa*), *na* for open places and events (*na lotnisko*, *na koncert*), and the fixed pairs follow the *w / na* rule you learned in unit 11.

**After do, the noun ends in -a or -u**: *dworzec → do dworca*, *sklep → do sklepu*, *dom → do domu*. This form is called *dopełniacz* and is the whole topic of unit 15. For now, just recognize the pattern.
**Tramwajem, pociągiem, autobusem** — vehicles take the *narzędnik* ending you've known since unit 8: "by tram", "by train". Ready-made formula: *jadę* + vehicle + *-em*.

**Za rogiem, po prawej stronie.** Directions use a mix of forms, and honestly there's no point unpacking them at this level. Learn them as chunks; the eight expressions in the extra section cover almost every situation.
**Chyba** means "I think, probably", and Poles use it constantly. It's not an awkward sign of doubt; it sounds natural and honest.
**Nie ma za co** — the standard reply to "thank you", literally "there's nothing for what". Its siblings: *proszę bardzo* and *drobiazg* ("a small thing").

grammars.title: Iść, jechać — and their routine partners
body: Polish uses different verbs for a trip that's **happening now** and one that's **repeated**. Four words, two pairs.

head: Now / this once
Habit / repeated
rows: *Idę do sklepu.* (I'm going to the shop now)
*Jadę do Warszawy.* (I'm on my way to Warsaw)

after: How to choose: if you can add "now" or "tomorrow" without it sounding odd, use *iść / jechać*. If the sentence has "always", "every day" or "often", use *chodzić / jeździć*.
⚠️ *Idę* is also used for near-future plans, just like English "I'm going": *Jutro idę do kina* — I'm going to the cinema tomorrow. Polish doesn't need a future form for this.
Motion verbs with prefixes (*przyjść*, *wyjść*, *pójść*, *dojść*) are a world of their own waiting in A2. You only need one now: *jak dojść do…?* — how do I get to…

grammars.title: Where to? — do, na, w
body: Destinations take different prepositions from locations, and the pairs are easy to remember side by side.

head: Where (unit 11)
Where to (this unit)
English
rows: in the shop / to the shop
at the post office / to the post office
at the airport / to the airport

after: The rule is neat: places that take *w* switch to **do**, places that take *na* keep **na** — only the noun ending changes, to the object form.
So you don't need to learn a new list at all. Whatever you decided in unit 11 still applies here.

head: Polski
Say it
English
rows: How do I get to… on foot?
How do I get to… by transport?
To the left / to the right
At the end of the street

blocks.title: If the directions are too fast
items: *Może pan pokazać na mapie?* — Could you show me on the map?
Don't be shy about using your phone: *Proszę napisać.* (please write it down) has rescued more foreigners than any memorized phrase.

sections.title: Vehicles and ways of getting around

blocks.text: Trams are the backbone of transport in Polish cities and are used far more than buses in Kraków, Wrocław and Poznań. The same ticket works on trams and buses, and it **must be validated** as soon as you board — in a small yellow or red machine near the door.

blocks.title: Phrases on public transport
items: *Czy ten autobus jedzie do centrum?* — Does this bus go to the center?
*Wysiadam na następnym.* — I'm getting off at the next one.
*Przepraszam, czy to miejsce jest wolne?* — Excuse me, is this seat free?
*Gdzie mogę skasować bilet?* — Where can I validate my ticket?
